claim: C. elegans TIR-1 is homologous to mammalian SARM1.
source: Here, we show that a phase transition of the Caenorhabditis elegans Toll/interleukin-1 receptor domain protein (TIR-1), an NAD+ glycohydrolase homologous to mammalian sterile alpha and TIR motif-containing 1 (SARM1), underlies p38 PMK-1 immune pathway activation in C. elegans intestinal epithelial cells.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract describing the relationship between TIR-1 and SARM1.

claim: TIR-1/SARM1 is an NAD+ glycohydrolase.
source: Here, we show that a phase transition of the Caenorhabditis elegans Toll/interleukin-1 receptor domain protein (TIR-1), an NAD+ glycohydrolase homologous to mammalian sterile alpha and TIR motif-containing 1 (SARM1), underlies p38 PMK-1 immune pathway activation in C. elegans intestinal epithelial cells.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract that TIR-1 is an NAD+ glycohydrolase.

claim: Pathogen infection induces multimerization of TIR-1/SARM1 into visible puncta within intestinal epithelial cells.
source: Through visualization of fluorescently labeled TIR-1/SARM1 protein, we demonstrate that physiologic stresses, both pathogen and non-pathogen, induce multimerization of TIR-1/SARM1 into visible puncta within intestinal epithelial cells.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract and supported by fluorescence microscopy data in Figure 1A.

claim: Cholesterol deficiency induces multimerization of TIR-1/SARM1 into visible puncta within intestinal epithelial cells.
source: Through visualization of fluorescently labeled TIR-1/SARM1 protein, we demonstrate that physiologic stresses, both pathogen and non-pathogen, induce multimerization of TIR-1/SARM1 into visible puncta within intestinal epithelial cells.
evidence: Stated in abstract as non-pathogen stress and demonstrated in Figure 5A showing puncta formation in nhr-8 mutants.

claim: The NAD+ glycohydrolase activity of C. elegans TIR-1 is dramatically potentiated by protein oligomerization.
source: In vitro enzyme kinetic analyses revealed that, like mammalian SARM1, the NAD+ glycohydrolase activity of C. elegans TIR-1 is dramatically potentiated by protein oligomerization and a phase transition.
evidence: Directly stated in abstract and supported by in vitro kinetic data in Figure 2.

claim: C. elegans with genetic mutations that block multimerization of TIR-1/SARM1 fail to induce p38 PMK phosphorylation.
source: Accordingly, C. elegans with genetic mutations that specifically block either multimerization or the NAD+ glycohydrolase activity of TIR-1/SARM1 fail to induce p38 PMK phosphorylation, are unable to increase immune effector expression, and are dramatically susceptible to bacterial infection.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by Western blot data in Figure 1E-F showing reduced phospho-PMK-1 in multimerization mutants.

claim: C. elegans with genetic mutations that block the NAD+ glycohydrolase activity of TIR-1/SARM1 fail to induce p38 PMK phosphorylation.
source: Accordingly, C. elegans with genetic mutations that specifically block either multimerization or the NAD+ glycohydrolase activity of TIR-1/SARM1 fail to induce p38 PMK phosphorylation, are unable to increase immune effector expression, and are dramatically susceptible to bacterial infection.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by Western blot data in Figure 1E-F showing reduced phospho-PMK-1 in catalytic mutant tir-1E788A.

claim: C. elegans with mutations blocking TIR-1/SARM1 multimerization are unable to increase immune effector expression.
source: Accordingly, C. elegans with genetic mutations that specifically block either multimerization or the NAD+ glycohydrolase activity of TIR-1/SARM1 fail to induce p38 PMK phosphorylation, are unable to increase immune effector expression, and are dramatically susceptible to bacterial infection.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by GFP reporter data in Figure 1D showing no T24B8.5p::gfp expression in multimerization mutants.

claim: C. elegans with mutations blocking TIR-1/SARM1 NAD+ glycohydrolase activity are unable to increase immune effector expression.
source: Accordingly, C. elegans with genetic mutations that specifically block either multimerization or the NAD+ glycohydrolase activity of TIR-1/SARM1 fail to induce p38 PMK phosphorylation, are unable to increase immune effector expression, and are dramatically susceptible to bacterial infection.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by GFP reporter data in Figure 1D showing no T24B8.5p::gfp expression in catalytic mutant.

claim: C. elegans with mutations blocking TIR-1/SARM1 multimerization are dramatically susceptible to bacterial infection.
source: Accordingly, C. elegans with genetic mutations that specifically block either multimerization or the NAD+ glycohydrolase activity of TIR-1/SARM1 fail to induce p38 PMK phosphorylation, are unable to increase immune effector expression, and are dramatically susceptible to bacterial infection.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by survival curve data in Figure 1G showing increased susceptibility to P. aeruginosa.

claim: C. elegans with mutations blocking TIR-1/SARM1 NAD+ glycohydrolase activity are dramatically susceptible to bacterial infection.
source: Accordingly, C. elegans with genetic mutations that specifically block either multimerization or the NAD+ glycohydrolase activity of TIR-1/SARM1 fail to induce p38 PMK phosphorylation, are unable to increase immune effector expression, and are dramatically susceptible to bacterial infection.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by survival curve data in Figure 1G showing increased susceptibility to P. aeruginosa.

claim: A loss-of-function mutation in nhr-8 causes TIR-1/SARM1 to oligomerize into puncta in intestinal epithelial cells.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that a loss-of-function mutation in nhr-8, which alters cholesterol metabolism and is used to study conditions of sterol deficiency, causes TIR-1/SARM1 to oligomerize into puncta in intestinal epithelial cells.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by fluorescence microscopy in Figure 5A showing puncta in nhr-8(hd117) mutants.

claim: nhr-8 alters cholesterol metabolism and is used to study conditions of sterol deficiency.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that a loss-of-function mutation in nhr-8, which alters cholesterol metabolism and is used to study conditions of sterol deficiency, causes TIR-1/SARM1 to oligomerize into puncta in intestinal epithelial cells.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by citation to Magner et al., 2013 in the introduction.

claim: Cholesterol scarcity increases p38 PMK-1 phosphorylation.
source: Cholesterol scarcity increases p38 PMK-1 phosphorylation, primes immune effector induction in a manner that requires TIR-1/SARM1 oligomerization and its intrinsic NAD+ glycohydrolase activity, and reduces pathogen accumulation in the intestine during a subsequent infection.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by Western blot data in Figure 4B-C showing increased phospho-PMK-1 in low cholesterol conditions.

claim: Cholesterol scarcity primes immune effector induction in a manner that requires TIR-1/SARM1 oligomerization.
source: Cholesterol scarcity increases p38 PMK-1 phosphorylation, primes immune effector induction in a manner that requires TIR-1/SARM1 oligomerization and its intrinsic NAD+ glycohydrolase activity, and reduces pathogen accumulation in the intestine during a subsequent infection.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by data in Figure 5C-F showing that multimerization mutants fail to induce immune effectors during cholesterol deprivation.

claim: Cholesterol scarcity primes immune effector induction in a manner that requires TIR-1/SARM1 NAD+ glycohydrolase activity.
source: Cholesterol scarcity increases p38 PMK-1 phosphorylation, primes immune effector induction in a manner that requires TIR-1/SARM1 oligomerization and its intrinsic NAD+ glycohydrolase activity, and reduces pathogen accumulation in the intestine during a subsequent infection.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by data in Figure 5C-F showing that catalytic mutant fails to induce immune effectors during cholesterol deprivation.

claim: Cholesterol scarcity reduces pathogen accumulation in the intestine during a subsequent infection.
source: Cholesterol scarcity increases p38 PMK-1 phosphorylation, primes immune effector induction in a manner that requires TIR-1/SARM1 oligomerization and its intrinsic NAD+ glycohydrolase activity, and reduces pathogen accumulation in the intestine during a subsequent infection.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by CFU data in Figure 3O showing reduced P. aeruginosa in nhr-8 mutants.

claim: A phase transition of TIR-1/SARM1 as a prerequisite for its NAD+ glycohydrolase activity is strongly conserved across millions of years of evolution.
source: Thus, a phase transition of TIR-1/SARM1 as a prerequisite for its NAD+ glycohydrolase activity is strongly conserved across millions of years of evolution and is essential for diverse physiological processes in multiple cell types.
evidence: Stated in abstract as a conclusion based on comparison with mammalian SARM1 data from Loring et al., 2021.

claim: A phase transition of TIR-1/SARM1 is essential for diverse physiological processes in multiple cell types.
source: Thus, a phase transition of TIR-1/SARM1 as a prerequisite for its NAD+ glycohydrolase activity is strongly conserved across millions of years of evolution and is essential for diverse physiological processes in multiple cell types.
evidence: Stated in abstract as a conclusion based on data showing TIR-1 function in intestinal immunity and comparison with neuronal degeneration.

claim: The C. elegans p38 homolog PMK-1 is part of a classic MAPK signaling cascade that is activated by the MAPKKK NSY-1 and MAPKK SEK-1.
source: The C. elegans p38 homolog PMK-1 is part of a classic MAPK signaling cascade that is activated by the MAPKKK NSY-1 and MAPKK SEK-1, which are the nematode homologs of mammalian ASK and MKK3/6, respectively (Kim et al., 2002).
evidence: Directly stated in introduction with citation to Kim et al., 2002.

claim: NSY-1 and SEK-1 are the nematode homologs of mammalian ASK and MKK3/6, respectively.
source: The C. elegans p38 homolog PMK-1 is part of a classic MAPK signaling cascade that is activated by the MAPKKK NSY-1 and MAPKK SEK-1, which are the nematode homologs of mammalian ASK and MKK3/6, respectively (Kim et al., 2002).
evidence: Directly stated in introduction with citation to Kim et al., 2002.

claim: The C. elegans p38 PMK-1 pathway regulates the expression of secreted innate immune effectors.
source: As in mammals, the C. elegans p38 PMK-1 pathway regulates the expression of secreted innate immune effectors and is required for survival during pathogen infection (Kim et al., 2002; Troemel et al., 2006; Peterson and Pukkila-Worley, 2018; Pukkila-Worley and Ausubel, 2012).
evidence: Directly stated in introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: The C. elegans p38 PMK-1 pathway is required for survival during pathogen infection.
source: As in mammals, the C. elegans p38 PMK-1 pathway regulates the expression of secreted innate immune effectors and is required for survival during pathogen infection (Kim et al., 2002; Troemel et al., 2006; Peterson and Pukkila-Worley, 2018; Pukkila-Worley and Ausubel, 2012).
evidence: Directly stated in introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: TIR-1 acts upstream of NSY-1/ASK to control p38 PMK-1 activation.
source: In C. elegans, TIR-1, the homolog of mammalian sterile alpha and TIR motif-containing 1 (SARM1), acts upstream of NSY-1/ASK to control p38 PMK-1 activation (Liberati et al., 2004; Couillault et al., 2004).
evidence: Directly stated in introduction with citations to Liberati et al., 2004 and Couillault et al., 2004.

claim: TIR-1/SARM1 is unique among animal and plant TIR domain-containing proteins in that it is an enzyme which cleaves NAD+.
source: Interestingly, TIR-1/SARM1 is unique among animal and plant TIR domain-containing proteins in that it is an enzyme, which cleaves nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) (Essuman et al., 2017; Wan et al., 2019).
evidence: Directly stated in introduction with citations to Essuman et al., 2017 and Wan et al., 2019.

claim: The NAD+ glycohydrolase activity of TIR is activated upon oligomerization into a multimeric protein complex.
source: The NAD+ glycohydrolase activity of TIR is activated upon oligomerization into a multimeric protein complex (Horsefield et al., 2019).
evidence: Directly stated in introduction with citation to Horsefield et al., 2019.

claim: NAD+ depletion by TIR promotes cell death in plants during pathogen infection.
source: NAD+ depletion in this manner promotes cell death in plants during pathogen infection and triggers axonal degeneration following neuronal injury (Gerdts et al., 2015; Gerdts et al., 2013).
evidence: Directly stated in introduction with citations to Gerdts et al., 2015 and 2013.

claim: NAD+ depletion by TIR triggers axonal degeneration following neuronal injury.
source: NAD+ depletion in this manner promotes cell death in plants during pathogen infection and triggers axonal degeneration following neuronal injury (Gerdts et al., 2015; Gerdts et al., 2013).
evidence: Directly stated in introduction with citations to Gerdts et al., 2015 and 2013.

claim: Human SARM1 oligomerizes and undergoes a phase transition, which enhances its intrinsic NAD+ glycohydrolase activity.
source: Interestingly, human SARM1 oligomerizes and undergoes a phase transition, which enhances its intrinsic NAD+ glycohydrolase activity (Loring et al., 2021).
evidence: Directly stated in introduction with citation to Loring et al., 2021.

claim: Induced multimerization of C. elegans TIR-1/SARM1 in neurons correlated with enhanced axonal degeneration.
source: Induced multimerization of C. elegans TIR-1/SARM1 in neurons also correlated with enhanced axonal degeneration (Loring et al., 2021).
evidence: Directly stated in introduction with citation to Loring et al., 2021.

claim: In uninfected animals, TIR-1::wrmScarlet is barely detectable in intestinal epithelial cells.
source: In uninfected animals, TIR-1::wrmScarlet is barely detectable in intestinal epithelial cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 1A microscopy images.

claim: P. aeruginosa infection caused TIR-1::wrmScarlet to multimerize into visible puncta within intestinal epithelial cells.
source: However, P. aeruginosa infection caused TIR-1::wrmScarlet to multimerize into visible puncta within intestinal epithelial cells (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 1A microscopy images and Figure 1B quantification.

claim: C. elegans TIR-1 protein has three characterized domains: a Heat/Armadillo repeat domain, a sterile alpha motif (SAM) domain, and a Toll-interleukin receptor (TIR) domain.
source: C. elegans TIR-1 protein has three characterized domains: a Heat/Armadillo repeat domain, a sterile alpha motif (SAM) domain, and a Toll-interleukin receptor (TIR) domain (Chuang and Bargmann, 2005; Figure 1C).
evidence: Directly stated in results with citation to Chuang and Bargmann, 2005, and shown in Figure 1C schematic.

claim: C. elegans TIR-1 oligomerizes in vitro through interactions of its SAM domains.
source: C. elegans TIR-1 oligomerizes in vitro through interactions of its SAM domains (Horsefield et al., 2019).
evidence: Directly stated in results with citation to Horsefield et al., 2019.

claim: The tir-1ΔSAM, tir-1G747P and tir-1H833A mutants prevented activation of the p38 PMK-1-dependent immune reporter T24B8.5p::gfp in animals infected with P. aeruginosa.
source: The C. elegans tir-1ΔSAM, tir-1G747P and tir-1H833A mutants prevented activation of the p38 PMK-1-dependent immune reporter T24B8.5p::gfp in animals infected with P. aeruginosa (Figure 1D).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 1D microscopy images.

claim: The tir-1ΔSAM, tir-1G747P and tir-1H833A mutants have reduced levels of active, phosphorylated p38 PMK-1, equivalent to the tir-1(qd4) null allele.
source: Consistent with these data, the tir-1ΔSAM, tir-1G747P and tir-1H833A mutants have reduced levels of active, phosphorylated p38 PMK-1, equivalent to the tir-1(qd4) null allele (Shivers et al., 2009; Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Directly stated in results with citation to Shivers et al., 2009, and shown in Figure 1E-F Western blot data.

claim: The tir-1ΔSAM, tir-1G747P and tir-1H833A mutants are each markedly hypersusceptible to P. aeruginosa infection.
source: Additionally, these mutants are each markedly hypersusceptible to P. aeruginosa infection (Figure 1G).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 1G survival curves.

claim: The TIR domain of C. elegans TIR-1 and its mammalian homolog SARM1 possess intrinsic NADase activity.
source: The TIR domain of C. elegans, TIR-1, and its mammalian homolog, SARM1, possess intrinsic NADase activity (Essuman et al., 2017; Horsefield et al., 2019; Summers et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated in results with citations to Essuman et al., 2017, Horsefield et al., 2019, and Summers et al., 2016.

claim: Oligomerization of mammalian SARM1 and C. elegans TIR-1 is required for maximal NADase activity in vitro.
source: Importantly, oligomerization of mammalian SARM1 and C. elegans TIR-1 is required for maximal NADase activity in vitro (Horsefield et al., 2019).
evidence: Directly stated in results with citation to Horsefield et al., 2019.

claim: The NADase activity in the TIR domain of mammalian SARM1 requires a putative catalytic glutamate residue.
source: The NADase activity in the TIR domain of mammalian SARM1 requires a putative catalytic glutamate residue (Essuman et al., 2017).
evidence: Directly stated in results with citation to Essuman et al., 2017.

claim: The tir-1E788A mutant does not induce T24B8.5p::gfp following P. aeruginosa infection.
source: We used CRISPR-Cas9 to mutate the homologous glutamate in C. elegans tir-1 (tir-1E788A) and found that it was required for the immunostimulatory activity of tir-1 – tir-1E788A mutants do not induce T24B8.5p::gfp following P. aeruginosa infection (Figure 1D), had less active, phosphorylated p38 PMK-1 (Figure 1E and F), and were more susceptible to P. aeruginosa infection (Figure 1G).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 1D microscopy images.

claim: The tir-1E788A mutant had less active, phosphorylated p38 PMK-1.
source: We used CRISPR-Cas9 to mutate the homologous glutamate in C. elegans tir-1 (tir-1E788A) and found that it was required for the immunostimulatory activity of tir-1 – tir-1E788A mutants do not induce T24B8.5p::gfp following P. aeruginosa infection (Figure 1D), had less active, phosphorylated p38 PMK-1 (Figure 1E and F), and were more susceptible to P. aeruginosa infection (Figure 1G).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 1E-F Western blot data.

claim: The tir-1E788A mutant was more susceptible to P. aeruginosa infection.
source: We used CRISPR-Cas9 to mutate the homologous glutamate in C. elegans tir-1 (tir-1E788A) and found that it was required for the immunostimulatory activity of tir-1 – tir-1E788A mutants do not induce T24B8.5p::gfp following P. aeruginosa infection (Figure 1D), had less active, phosphorylated p38 PMK-1 (Figure 1E and F), and were more susceptible to P. aeruginosa infection (Figure 1G).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 1G survival curves.

claim: Purified TIR only shows very modest NADase activity even at high protein concentrations (>15 μM).
source: Interestingly, purified TIR only shows very modest NADase activity even at high protein concentrations ( > 15 μM) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2A enzyme kinetics data.

claim: The NADase activity of TIR increased parabolically with increasing TIR concentrations rather than linearly.
source: Notably, the NADase activity of TIR increased parabolically with increasing TIR concentrations rather than linearly, suggesting that multimerization of TIR-1 potentiates its NADase activity (Figure 2A).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2A enzyme kinetics data.

claim: Multimerization of TIR-1 potentiates its NADase activity.
source: Notably, the NADase activity of TIR increased parabolically with increasing TIR concentrations rather than linearly, suggesting that multimerization of TIR-1 potentiates its NADase activity (Figure 2A).
evidence: Stated as inference from the parabolic concentration dependence shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Macroviscogens (PEG 3350 and PEG 8000) dramatically increased the NADase activity of TIR.
source: Interestingly, macroviscogens (polyethylene glycol [PEG] 3350 and PEG 8000), but not microviscogens (sucrose or glycerol), dramatically increased the NADase activity of TIR (Figure 2B).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2B enzyme activity data.

claim: Microviscogens (sucrose or glycerol) did not dramatically increase the NADase activity of TIR.
source: Interestingly, macroviscogens (polyethylene glycol [PEG] 3350 and PEG 8000), but not microviscogens (sucrose or glycerol), dramatically increased the NADase activity of TIR (Figure 2B).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2B enzyme activity data.

claim: Treatment with smaller molecular weight PEGs (e.g. PEG 1500 and PEG 400) did not increase the enzymatic activity of TIR.
source: These effects were most pronounced with higher molecular weight PEGs, as treatment with smaller molecular weight PEGs (e.g. PEG 1500 and PEG 400) did not increase the enzymatic activity of TIR (Figure 2C).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2C dose-response data.

claim: PEGs 3350 and 8000 increase TIR activity in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Specifically, PEGs 3350 and 8000 increase TIR activity in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 2C).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2C dose-response data.

claim: Crowding agents increase the activity of the TIR domain of human SARM1, as well as plant TIR domains.
source: Crowding agents also increase the activity of the TIR domain of human SARM1, as well as plant TIR domains (Horsefield et al., 2019; Loring et al., 2021), suggesting that the mechanism of TIR regulation is strongly conserved.
evidence: Directly stated in results with citations to Horsefield et al., 2019 and Loring et al., 2021.

claim: The mechanism of TIR regulation is strongly conserved.
source: Crowding agents also increase the activity of the TIR domain of human SARM1, as well as plant TIR domains (Horsefield et al., 2019; Loring et al., 2021), suggesting that the mechanism of TIR regulation is strongly conserved.
evidence: Stated as inference from the observation that crowding agents activate TIR domains across species.

claim: Treatment with 25% PEG 3350 led to a roughly linear association between TIR concentration and NADase activity.
source: Treatment with 25% PEG 3350 led to a roughly linear association between TIR concentration and NADase activity and markedly enhanced TIR activity at each enzyme concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The Km of TIR increases and then decreases to level off at ~500 μM of ε-NAD with increasing concentration of PEG 3350.
source: The Km of TIR increases and then decreases to level off at ~500 μM of ε-NAD with increasing concentration of PEG 3350 (Figure 2E).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2E kinetic parameter data.

claim: kcat increases nearly linearly with increasing concentrations of PEG 3350.
source: On the other hand, kcat increases nearly linearly with increasing concentrations of PEG 3350 (Figure 2F).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2F kinetic parameter data.

claim: The catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) followed the same trend as kcat, indicating that increased TIR activity is due to increased substrate turnover by the enzyme and not tighter substrate binding.
source: In addition, the catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) followed the same trend as kcat, indicating that increased TIR activity is due to increased substrate turnover by the enzyme and not tighter substrate binding (Figure 2G).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2G kinetic parameter data.

claim: The NAD hydrolase activity of TIR is also activated by the precipitant sodium citrate.
source: We found that the NAD hydrolase activity of TIR is also activated by the precipitant sodium citrate, providing an orthologous method to characterize the enzymatic activity of the TIR domain (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The response to increasing citrate concentration was switch-like, where a concentration of at least 250 mM sodium citrate was needed to observe enzyme activity.
source: Notably, the response to increasing citrate concentration was switch-like, where a concentration of at least 250 mM sodium citrate was needed to observe enzyme activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Activation with PEG 3350 was more dose-dependent than activation with citrate.
source: By contrast, activation with PEG 3350 was more dose-dependent (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Directly stated in results comparing PEG and citrate activation, shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: At high concentrations of both PEG and citrate, TIR was principally located in the pelleted (insoluble) fraction.
source: At low concentrations of both PEG and citrate, TIR protein was present in the supernatant. However, at high concentrations of both PEG and citrate, TIR was principally located in the pelleted (insoluble) fraction, as visualized by Coomassie staining on an SDS-PAGE gel (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G gel images.

claim: Robust NADase activity was observed in the pelleted fraction and not in the supernatant of samples treated with high concentrations of PEG or citrate.
source: Importantly, robust NADase activity was observed in the pelleted fraction and not in the supernatant of samples treated with high concentrations of PEG or citrate (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G activity data.

claim: Precipitation/aggregation of TIR is required to activate the intrinsic NADase activity of TIR-1/SARM1.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that precipitation/aggregation of TIR is required to activate the intrinsic NADase activity of TIR-1/SARM1.
evidence: Stated as conclusion from precipitation and activity correlation data in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: TIRG747P and TIRE788Q mutants showed no apparent activity.
source: Notably, TIRG747P and TIRE788Q mutants showed no apparent activity, and TIRE788A and TIRH833A showed a > 1 × 108­fold decrease in catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) compared to TIRWT (Figure 2I).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2I kinetic data.

claim: TIRE788A and TIRH833A showed a >1 × 10^8-fold decrease in catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) compared to TIRWT.
source: Notably, TIRG747P and TIRE788Q mutants showed no apparent activity, and TIRE788A and TIRH833A showed a > 1 × 108­fold decrease in catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) compared to TIRWT (Figure 2I).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2I kinetic data.

claim: TIRG747P was unable to precipitate as readily as TIRWT.
source: Consistent with our genetic data, TIRG747P, which contains a mutation that prevents oligomerization of TIR, was unable to precipitate as readily as TIRWT (Figure 2J).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2J precipitation data.

claim: Compared to TIRWT, the TIRG747P mutant in the presence of PEG 3350 demonstrated a 25% decrease in the amount of precipitated protein.
source: Compared to TIRWT, the TIRG747P mutant in the presence of PEG 3350 demonstrated a 25% decrease in the amount of precipitated protein (Figure 2J).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2J quantification.

claim: TIR proteins with two different mutations in the glutamate required for NAD+ catalysis, TIRE788A and TIRE788Q, precipitated to a similar extent as TIRWT.
source: Importantly, TIR proteins with two different mutations in the glutamate required for NAD+ catalysis, TIRE788A and TIRE788Q, precipitated to a similar extent as TIRWT (Figure 2J and K, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1I and J) but had minimal NADase activity (Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2J, K and supplement figures.

claim: TIRE788A and TIRE788Q had minimal NADase activity.
source: Importantly, TIR proteins with two different mutations in the glutamate required for NAD+ catalysis, TIRE788A and TIRE788Q, precipitated to a similar extent as TIRWT (Figure 2J and K, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1I and J) but had minimal NADase activity (Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: A phase transition of TIR-1 is required for its NADase activity.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that a phase transition of TIR-1 is required for its NADase activity.
evidence: Stated as conclusion from mutant precipitation and activity data.

claim: 1,6-hexanediol decreases the NADase activity of TIR by <2 fold in the presence of either PEG 3350 or citrate.
source: In the presence of either PEG 3350 or citrate, we observed that 1,6-hexanediol decreases the NADase activity of TIR by <2 fold (Figure 2L).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2L activity data.

claim: The NADase activity of TIR is predominantly associated with a solid, rather than a liquid, state or lies on a continuum between a liquid-like and solid-like state.
source: While significant, this modest decrease (the activity of 1,6-hexanediol-treated TIR remains two orders of magnitude higher than the activity of TIR without PEG 3350 or citrate addition) suggests that the NADase activity of TIR is predominantly associated with a solid, rather than a liquid, state or lies on a continuum between a liquid-like and solid-like state (Figure 2L).
evidence: Stated as inference from the modest effect of 1,6-hexanediol on TIR activity shown in Figure 2L.

claim: In the absence of PEG 3350 or citrate, the low-level TIR NADase activity can be inhibited by 1,6-hexanediol.
source: Notably, in the absence of PEG 3350 or citrate, the low-level TIR NADase activity can be inhibited by 1,6-hexanediol (Figure 2L), suggesting that this activity is driven by hydrophobic interactions.
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2L activity data.

claim: The low-level TIR NADase activity in the absence of PEG or citrate is driven by hydrophobic interactions.
source: Notably, in the absence of PEG 3350 or citrate, the low-level TIR NADase activity can be inhibited by 1,6-hexanediol (Figure 2L), suggesting that this activity is driven by hydrophobic interactions.
evidence: Stated as inference from the inhibition by 1,6-hexanediol shown in Figure 2L.

claim: 1,6-hexanediol does not interfere with TIR precipitation in the presence of PEG or citrate.
source: Importantly, 1,6-hexanediol does not interfere with TIR precipitation in the presence of PEG or citrate, regardless of whether it is added before or after precipitate formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The phase transition of TIR is partially reversible in PEG 3350.
source: These data indicate that the phase transition of TIR is partially reversible in PEG 3350 and irreversible in sodium citrate.
evidence: Stated as conclusion from resuspension experiments and confirmed by SDS-PAGE in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The phase transition of TIR is irreversible in sodium citrate.
source: These data indicate that the phase transition of TIR is partially reversible in PEG 3350 and irreversible in sodium citrate.
evidence: Stated as conclusion from resuspension experiments and confirmed by SDS-PAGE in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: In the presence of 25% PEG, TIR precipitation increased with increasing pH.
source: However, in the presence of 25% PEG, TIR precipitation increased with increasing pH (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Under conditions with 25% PEG, no TIR activity was apparent below pH 6.
source: Under these same conditions, no activity was apparent below pH 6, Km remained constant (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E), and kcat increased from pH 6.5 to pH 8.5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E-F.

claim: In the absence of citrate, borderline fibrillar structures and protein aggregates were observed, but overall there were no consistent structures.
source: In the absence of citrate, we observed borderline fibrillar structures and protein aggregates, but overall, there were no consistent structures (Figure 2N).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2N electron microscopy images.

claim: In the presence of citrate, circular TIR particles emerged.
source: However, in the presence of citrate, circular particles emerged (Figure 2N).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2N electron microscopy images.

claim: C. elegans is a sterol auxotroph and requires dietary sterols for development, lifespan, fecundity, and resistance to pathogen infection.
source: C. elegans is a sterol auxotroph and requires dietary sterols for development, lifespan, fecundity, and resistance to pathogen infection (Hieb and Rothstein, 1968; Chitwood, 1999; Shim et al., 2002; Merris et al., 2003; Yochem et al., 1999; Otarigho and Aballay, 2020; Cheong et al., 2011).
evidence: Directly stated in results with multiple supporting citations.

claim: C. elegans grown in the absence of cholesterol supplementation activated GFP-based transcriptional reporters for T24B8.5p::gfp and irg-5p::gfp.
source: We found that C. elegans grown in the absence of cholesterol supplementation activated GFP-based transcriptional reporters for two putative immune effector genes, T24B8.5p::gfp and irg-5p::gfp (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 3A and B microscopy images.

claim: T24B8.5 and irg-5 are expressed in the intestine, induced during infection with multiple pathogens including P. aeruginosa, and controlled by the p38 PMK-1 innate immune pathway.
source: T24B8.5 and irg-5 are expressed in the intestine, induced during infection with multiple pathogens, including P. aeruginosa, and controlled by the p38 PMK-1 innate immune pathway (Troemel et al., 2006; Shivers et al., 2009; Bolz et al., 2010).
evidence: Directly stated in results with citations to Troemel et al., 2006, Shivers et al., 2009, and Bolz et al., 2010.

claim: C. elegans in a low cholesterol environment upregulate T24B8.5, irg-5, irg-4, and K08D8.4.
source: qRT-PCR studies confirmed that C. elegans in a low cholesterol environment upregulate T24B8.5 and irg-5, as well as other innate immune effector genes (irg-4 and K08D8.4) (Figure 3C).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 3C qRT-PCR data.

claim: Host defense pathways are activated in the absence of pathogen infection when environmental sterols are scarce.
source: These data suggest that host defense pathways are activated in the absence of pathogen infection when environmental sterols are scarce.
evidence: Stated as inference from the observation that immune genes are upregulated during cholesterol deprivation.

claim: The nuclear hormone receptor NHR-8 is a homolog of mammalian liver X receptor (LXR) and pregnane X receptor (PXR).
source: The nuclear hormone receptor, NHR-8, a homolog of mammalian liver X receptor (LXR) and pregnane X receptor (PXR), is required for the transport, distribution, and metabolism of cholesterol in C. elegans (Magner et al., 2013; Lindblom et al., 2001).
evidence: Directly stated in results with citations to Magner et al., 2013 and Lindblom et al., 2001.

claim: NHR-8 is required for the transport, distribution, and metabolism of cholesterol in C. elegans.
source: The nuclear hormone receptor, NHR-8, a homolog of mammalian liver X receptor (LXR) and pregnane X receptor (PXR), is required for the transport, distribution, and metabolism of cholesterol in C. elegans (Magner et al., 2013; Lindblom et al., 2001).
evidence: Directly stated in results with citations to Magner et al., 2013 and Lindblom et al., 2001.

claim: The transcription profile of nhr-8(hd117) and nhr-8(ok186) animals mimics that of wild-type C. elegans infected with P. aeruginosa.
source: Notably, the transcription profile of nhr-8(hd117) and nhr-8(ok186) animals mimics that of wild-type C. elegans infected with the bacterial pathogen P. aeruginosa (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A correlation plots.

claim: Innate immune effectors were strongly enriched among genes that were transcriptionally activated during cholesterol deprivation.
source: Consistent with our transcriptome profiling experiments of nhr-8 loss-of-function mutants, we discovered that innate immune effectors were strongly enriched among genes that were transcriptionally activated during cholesterol deprivation (Figure 3E).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 3E correlation plot.

claim: The expression of innate immune effectors was significantly correlated in wild-type animals infected with P. aeruginosa and in wild-type nematodes starved for cholesterol (r = 0.610).
source: Specifically, the expression of innate immune effectors was significantly correlated in wild-type animals infected with P. aeruginosa and in wild-type nematodes starved for cholesterol (r = 0.610) (Figure 3E).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 3E correlation plot.

claim: Supplementation of exogenous cholesterol at an increased concentration (80 μg/mL) fully suppressed T24B8.5p::gfp activation in the nhr-8(hd117) mutant.
source: First, supplementation of exogenous cholesterol at an increased concentration (80 μg/mL) fully suppressed T24B8.5p::gfp activation in the nhr-8(hd117) mutant (Figure 3F).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 3F microscopy images.

claim: Supplementation with Tergitol or Triton X-100 suppressed T24B8.5p::gfp activation in nhr-8(hd117) animals in a manner that was dependent on the presence of added cholesterol in the growth media.
source: Second, supplementation with the non-ionic detergents Tergitol or Triton X-100, which solubilize hydrophobic, amphipathic compounds, including sterols, suppressed T24B8.5p::gfp activation in nhr-8(hd117) animals in a manner that was dependent on the presence of added cholesterol in the growth media (Figure 3G and H, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 3G, H and supplement figure.

claim: On agarose, the addition of Tergitol to the growth media suppressed T24B8.5p::gfp activation in the nhr-8(hd117) mutant, but only in the presence of 5 μg/mL of cholesterol.
source: Importantly, on agarose, the addition of Tergitol to the growth media also suppressed T24B8.5p::gfp activation in the nhr-8(hd117) mutant, but only in the presence of 5 μg/mL of cholesterol (Figure 3H).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 3H microscopy images.

claim: Solubilization of cholesterol by Tergitol in standard nematode growth media suppresses immune activation in the nhr-8(hd117) mutant background.
source: These data establish that solubilization of cholesterol by Tergitol in standard nematode growth media suppresses immune activation in the nhr-8(hd117) mutant background.
evidence: Stated as conclusion from Tergitol supplementation experiments.

claim: Tergitol suppressed activation of T24B8.5, irg-4, irg-5, and K08D8.4 in the nhr-8(hd117) mutant.
source: We used qRT-PCR to confirm these findings – Tergitol suppressed activation of T24B8.5, as well as the immune effectors irg-4, irg-5, and K08D8.4 in the nhr-8(hd117) mutant (Figure 3I–L).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 3I-L qRT-PCR data.

claim: Activation of immune defenses in nhr-8(hd117) animals is specific to cholesterol deprivation.
source: Of note, activation of immune defenses in nhr-8(hd117) animals is specific to cholesterol deprivation in this genetic background, as supplementation with individual saturated, mono- and polyunsaturated fatty acids, which are also misregulated in the nhr-8(hd117) mutant background (Magner et al., 2013), failed to suppress activation of T24B8.5p::gfp (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Directly stated in results with citation to Magner et al., 2013, and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Wild-type C. elegans raised on media without supplemented cholesterol are hypersusceptible to killing by P. aeruginosa.
source: It has been previously shown that wild-type C. elegans raised on media without supplemented cholesterol are hypersusceptible to killing by P. aeruginosa, as are nhr-8(hd117) mutants on media with standard cholesterol supplementation (5 μg/mL) (Otarigho and Aballay, 2020).
evidence: Directly stated in results with citation to Otarigho and Aballay, 2020.

claim: nhr-8(hd117) mutants on media with standard cholesterol supplementation (5 μg/mL) are hypersusceptible to killing by P. aeruginosa.
source: It has been previously shown that wild-type C. elegans raised on media without supplemented cholesterol are hypersusceptible to killing by P. aeruginosa, as are nhr-8(hd117) mutants on media with standard cholesterol supplementation (5 μg/mL) (Otarigho and Aballay, 2020).
evidence: Directly stated in results with citation to Otarigho and Aballay, 2020.

claim: High doses of cholesterol (80 μg/mL) rescued the enhanced susceptibility of nhr-8(hd117) mutants to P. aeruginosa infection.
source: Importantly, we found that high doses of cholesterol (80 μg/mL) rescued the enhanced susceptibility of nhr-8(hd117) mutants to P. aeruginosa infection (Figure 3M).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 3M survival curves.

claim: Tergitol and Triton X-100, which solubilize cholesterol in nematode growth media, restored wild-type pathogen resistance to the nhr-8(hd117) mutant.
source: We confirmed this finding using an orthologous approach. Two detergents (Tergitol or Triton X-100), which solubilize cholesterol in nematode growth media, also restored wild-type pathogen resistance to the nhr-8(hd117) mutant (Figure 3N), consistent with their ability to modulate the expression of innate immune effectors (Figure 3G–L).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 3N survival curves.

claim: The nhr-8(hd117) mutant accumulated less P. aeruginosa in its intestine during infection than wild-type animals.
source: Importantly, we found that the nhr-8(hd117) mutant accumulated less P. aeruginosa in its intestine during infection than wild-type animals (Figure 3O).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 3O CFU quantification.

claim: Low cholesterol in the nhr-8(hd117) mutants reduces tolerance to pathogen infection.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that low cholesterol in the nhr-8(hd117) mutants reduces tolerance to pathogen infection, and that the robust transcriptional induction of immune effectors in this mutant background leads to reduced accumulation of P. aeruginosa during infection.
evidence: Stated as inference from the observation that nhr-8 mutants are susceptible to infection despite reduced pathogen burden.

claim: The robust transcriptional induction of immune effectors in the nhr-8(hd117) mutant background leads to reduced accumulation of P. aeruginosa during infection.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that low cholesterol in the nhr-8(hd117) mutants reduces tolerance to pathogen infection, and that the robust transcriptional induction of immune effectors in this mutant background leads to reduced accumulation of P. aeruginosa during infection.
evidence: Stated as inference from the observation that nhr-8 mutants have high immune gene expression and low pathogen burden.

claim: Targets of the p38 PMK-1 innate immune pathway were strongly enriched among the genes induced in wild-type animals during cholesterol deprivation.
source: Additional analyses of the transcriptome profiling data revealed that targets of the p38 PMK-1 innate immune pathway were strongly enriched among the genes induced in wild-type animals during cholesterol deprivation (Figure 4A).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 4A GSEA plot.

claim: The levels of active, phosphorylated PMK-1 were higher in wild-type animals grown on media without supplemented cholesterol than in animals grown under standard culture conditions.
source: Accordingly, the levels of active, phosphorylated PMK-1 were higher in wild-type animals grown on media without supplemented cholesterol than in animals grown under standard culture conditions (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 4B-C Western blot data.

claim: The p38 PMK-1 pathway is activated in nhr-8 loss-of-function mutants.
source: Consistent with these data, the p38 PMK-1 pathway is also activated in nhr-8 loss-of-function mutants.
evidence: Stated as conclusion from GSEA and Western blot data in Figure 4D-F.

claim: The nhr-8(hd117) and nhr-8(ok186) mutants had an increased ratio of phosphorylated PMK-1 relative to total PMK-1 compared to wild-type controls.
source: In addition, the nhr-8(hd117) and nhr-8(ok186) mutants had an increased ratio of phosphorylated PMK-1 relative to total PMK-1 compared to wild-type controls (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 4E-F Western blot data.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of tir-1 fully suppressed hyperactivation of T24B8.5p::gfp in nhr-8(hd117) animals.
source: RNAi-mediated knockdown of tir-1, the most upstream component of the p38 signaling cassette (Liberati et al., 2004; Couillault et al., 2004), fully suppressed hyperactivation of T24B8.5p::gfp in nhr-8(hd117) animals (Figure 4G).
evidence: Directly stated in results with citations and shown in Figure 4G microscopy images.

claim: The tir-1(qd4) loss-of-function mutation completely suppressed the induction of T24B8.5, irg-4, irg-5, and K08D8.4 in the nhr-8(hd117) background.
source: The tir-1(qd4) loss-of-function mutation completely suppressed the induction of T24B8.5, irg-4, irg-5, and K08D8.4 in the nhr-8(hd117) background (Figure 4H–K).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 4H-K qRT-PCR data.

claim: In nhr-8(hd117) animals, knockdown of atf-7, but not skn-1, abrogated T24B8.5p::gfp activation.
source: In nhr-8(hd117) animals, knockdown of atf-7, but not skn-1, abrogated T24B8.5p::gfp activation (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 4G and supplement figures.

claim: Solubilization of cholesterol with Tergitol was unable to suppress activation of T24B8.5p::gfp induced by knockdown of vhp-1.
source: Finally, to further support our observation that cholesterol scarcity induces immune defenses upstream of p38 PMK-1, we used the MAPK phosphatase vhp-1, a negative regulator of PMK-1 (Kim et al., 2004). Solubilization of cholesterol with Tergitol was unable to suppress activation of T24B8.5p::gfp induced by knockdown of vhp-1 (Figure 4L).
evidence: Directly stated in results with citation to Kim et al., 2004, and shown in Figure 4L microscopy images.

claim: Cholesterol scarcity induces immune defenses upstream of p38 PMK-1.
source: Finally, to further support our observation that cholesterol scarcity induces immune defenses upstream of p38 PMK-1, we used the MAPK phosphatase vhp-1, a negative regulator of PMK-1 (Kim et al., 2004).
evidence: Stated as conclusion supported by vhp-1 epistasis experiment in Figure 4L.

claim: tir-1(qd4);nhr-8(hd117) double mutants were more susceptible to P. aeruginosa infection than nhr-8(hd117) mutants.
source: Interestingly, tir-1(qd4);nhr-8(hd117) double mutants were more susceptible to P. aeruginosa infection than nhr-8(hd117) mutants (Figure 4M).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 4M survival curves.

claim: The induction of the p38 PMK-1 pathway in the nhr-8(hd117) mutant background promotes resistance to P. aeruginosa infection.
source: These data suggest that the induction of the p38 PMK-1 pathway in the nhr-8(hd117) mutant background promotes resistance to P. aeruginosa infection.
evidence: Stated as inference from the observation that tir-1;nhr-8 double mutants are more susceptible than nhr-8 single mutants.

claim: tir-1(qd4);nhr-8(hd117) double mutants were slightly, but significantly and reproducibly, more susceptible than the tir-1(qd4) mutant to killing by P. aeruginosa.
source: In addition, tir-1(qd4);nhr-8(hd117) double mutants were slightly, but significantly and reproducibly, more susceptible than the tir-1(qd4) mutant to killing by P. aeruginosa.
evidence: Directly stated in results referring to Figure 4M survival data.

claim: The inherent susceptibility to pathogen-mediated killing in animals that lack sufficient cholesterol leads to additive pathogen susceptibility in animals that also lack a functioning p38 PMK-1 host defense pathway.
source: We therefore hypothesize that the inherent susceptibility to pathogen-mediated killing in animals that lack sufficient cholesterol (e.g. the nhr-8(hd117) mutant) leads to additive pathogen susceptibility in animals that also lack a functioning p38 PMK-1 host defense pathway (e.g. the tir-1(qd4) mutant).
evidence: Stated as hypothesis to explain the additive susceptibility of double mutants.

claim: nhr-8(hd117) mutant animals induced TIR-1::wrmScarlet puncta formation in intestinal epithelial cells.
source: Consistent with our studies during P. aeruginosa infection (Figure 1A), nhr-8(hd117) mutant animals induced TIR-1::wrmScarlet puncta formation in intestinal epithelial cells (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 5A-B microscopy and quantification.

claim: TIR-1::wrmScarlet puncta formation in nhr-8(hd117) animals was entirely suppressed by solubilizing cholesterol in the growth media with Tergitol.
source: Importantly, TIR-1::wrmScarlet puncta formation in nhr-8(hd117) animals was entirely suppressed by solubilizing cholesterol in the growth media with Tergitol (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 5A-B microscopy and quantification.

claim: Treatment of nhr-8(hd117) animals expressing TIR-1::wrmScarlet with tir-1(RNAi) inhibited fluorescence and puncta formation.
source: Additionally, treatment of nhr-8(hd117) animals expressing TIR-1::wrmScarlet with tir-1(RNAi) inhibited fluorescence and puncta formation (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 5A-B microscopy and quantification.

claim: The C. elegans tir-1ΔSAM, tir-1G747P and tir-1H833A mutants prevented activation of the p38 PMK-1-dependent immune reporter T24B8.5p::gfp in nhr-8(RNAi) animals.
source: Importantly, the C. elegans tir-1ΔSAM, tir-1G747P and tir-1H833A mutants, which contain specific mutations that block oligomerization of TIR-1, and the tir-1E788A strain that carries a mutation in the catalytic glutamine required for the NADase activity, each prevented activation of the p38 PMK-1-dependent immune reporter T24B8.5p::gfp in nhr-8(RNAi) animals (Figure 5C) and during cholesterol deprivation (Figure 5D).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 5C microscopy images.

claim: The tir-1E788A strain prevented activation of the p38 PMK-1-dependent immune reporter T24B8.5p::gfp in nhr-8(RNAi) animals.
source: Importantly, the C. elegans tir-1ΔSAM, tir-1G747P and tir-1H833A mutants, which contain specific mutations that block oligomerization of TIR-1, and the tir-1E788A strain that carries a mutation in the catalytic glutamine required for the NADase activity, each prevented activation of the p38 PMK-1-dependent immune reporter T24B8.5p::gfp in nhr-8(RNAi) animals (Figure 5C) and during cholesterol deprivation (Figure 5D).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 5C microscopy images.

claim: The tir-1ΔSAM, tir-1G747P, tir-1H833A, and tir-1E788A mutants prevented activation of T24B8.5p::gfp during cholesterol deprivation.
source: Importantly, the C. elegans tir-1ΔSAM, tir-1G747P and tir-1H833A mutants, which contain specific mutations that block oligomerization of TIR-1, and the tir-1E788A strain that carries a mutation in the catalytic glutamine required for the NADase activity, each prevented activation of the p38 PMK-1-dependent immune reporter T24B8.5p::gfp in nhr-8(RNAi) animals (Figure 5C) and during cholesterol deprivation (Figure 5D).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 5D microscopy images.

claim: Mutations in tir-1 that block oligomerization or NADase activity abrogated the induction of T24B8.5 and irg-4 immune effectors in nhr-8(RNAi) animals.
source: Using qRT-PCR, we confirmed that these mutations in tir-1 abrogated the induction of the T24B8.5 (Figure 5E) and irg-4 (Figure 5F) immune effectors in nhr-8(RNAi) animals.
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 5E-F qRT-PCR data.

claim: tir-1 mutants phenocopied the effects of the p38 PMK-1 pathway mutants on the basal expression of immune effector genes.
source: We also found that these tir-1 mutants phenocopied the effects of the p38 PMK-1 pathway mutants (tir-1(qd4), nys-1(ag3), and pmk-1(km25)) on the basal expression of these immune effector genes (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 5E-F qRT-PCR data.

claim: Physiological stresses, both pathogen and non-pathogen, induce TIR-1 multimerization into puncta within intestinal epithelial cells, which then activates the p38 PMK-1 innate immune pathway through the intrinsic NADase activity of the TIR-1 protein complex.
source: In summary, the above data demonstrate for the first time that physiological stresses, both pathogen and non-pathogen, induce TIR-1 multimerization into puncta within intestinal epithelial cells, which then activates the p38 PMK-1 innate immune pathway through the intrinsic NADase activity of the TIR-1 protein complex.
evidence: Stated as summary conclusion from all the data presented in the results section.

claim: The induction of irg-4p::gfp during P. aeruginosa infection was enhanced when nematodes were infected on media that did not contain supplemented cholesterol.
source: Interestingly, the induction of irg-4p::gfp (Figure 6A), irg-5p::gfp (Figure 6B), and T24B8.5p::gfp (Figure 6C) during P. aeruginosa infection was enhanced when nematodes were infected on media that did not contain supplemented cholesterol.
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 6A microscopy images.

claim: The induction of irg-5p::gfp during P. aeruginosa infection was enhanced when nematodes were infected on media that did not contain supplemented cholesterol.
source: Interestingly, the induction of irg-4p::gfp (Figure 6A), irg-5p::gfp (Figure 6B), and T24B8.5p::gfp (Figure 6C) during P. aeruginosa infection was enhanced when nematodes were infected on media that did not contain supplemented cholesterol.
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 6B microscopy images.

claim: The induction of T24B8.5p::gfp during P. aeruginosa infection was enhanced when nematodes were infected on media that did not contain supplemented cholesterol.
source: Interestingly, the induction of irg-4p::gfp (Figure 6A), irg-5p::gfp (Figure 6B), and T24B8.5p::gfp (Figure 6C) during P. aeruginosa infection was enhanced when nematodes were infected on media that did not contain supplemented cholesterol.
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 6C microscopy images.

claim: P. aeruginosa infection led to increased activation of irg-4p::gfp when nhr-8 was depleted by RNAi.
source: Consistent with these data, P. aeruginosa infection also led to increased activation of irg-4p::gfp (Figure 6D) and irg-5p::gfp (Figure 6E) when nhr-8 was depleted by RNAi.
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 6D microscopy images.

claim: P. aeruginosa infection led to increased activation of irg-5p::gfp when nhr-8 was depleted by RNAi.
source: Consistent with these data, P. aeruginosa infection also led to increased activation of irg-4p::gfp (Figure 6D) and irg-5p::gfp (Figure 6E) when nhr-8 was depleted by RNAi.
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 6E microscopy images.

claim: p38 PMK-1-dependent genes were strongly enriched among Cluster I genes.
source: Importantly, p38 PMK-1-dependent genes were strongly enriched among Cluster I, but not Cluster II, genes (Figure 6G).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 6G enrichment analysis.

claim: Thirty-three of the 139 genes in Cluster I are known targets of the p38 PMK-1 immune pathway (24.17-fold enriched, hypergeometric P-value = 7.68 x 10^-37).
source: Thirty-three of the 139 genes in Cluster I are known targets of the p38 PMK-1 immune pathway (24.17-fold enriched, hypergeometric P-value = 7.68 x 10–37), a group that includes the immune effectors T24B8.5 (Figure 6H), irg-4 (Figure 6I), irg-5 (Figure 6J), and K08D8.4 (Figure 6K).
evidence: Directly stated in results with statistical values and shown in Figure 6G-K.

claim: Only three genes in Cluster II are p38 PMK-1-dependent transcripts (6.95-fold enriched, hypergeometric p-value = 0.01).
source: By contrast, only three genes in Cluster II are p38 PMK-1-dependent transcripts (6.95-fold enriched, hypergeometric p-value = 0.01) (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: Directly stated in results with statistical values and shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: Sterol scarcity primes the induction of innate immune effectors by activating the p38 PMK-1 immune pathway.
source: These data demonstrate that sterol scarcity primes the induction of innate immune effectors by activating the p38 PMK-1 immune pathway.
evidence: Stated as conclusion from the clustering and enrichment analysis of infection response genes.

claim: Subsequent challenge by P. aeruginosa further drives immune activation in a manner that leads to reduced pathogen accumulation in the intestine.
source: Subsequent challenge by P. aeruginosa further drives immune activation in a manner that leads to reduced pathogen accumulation in the intestine (Figure 3O).
evidence: Stated as conclusion referring to CFU data in Figure 3O.

claim: A phase transition of C. elegans TIR-1 underlies p38 PMK-1 immune pathway activation in the C. elegans intestine.
source: Here, we report two conceptual advances. First, we show that a phase transition of C. elegans TIR-1, an NADase homologous to mammalian SARM1, underlies p38 PMK-1 immune pathway activation in the C. elegans intestine (Figure 6L).
evidence: Stated as main conclusion in discussion and shown in model Figure 6L.

claim: Cholesterol deficiency causes TIR-1/SARM1 to oligomerize into puncta in intestinal epithelial cells and activate the p38 PMK-1 immune pathway through its intrinsic NADase activity.
source: Second, we show that cholesterol deficiency, as recapitulated in an nhr-8 loss-of-function mutant, causes TIR-1/SARM1 to oligomerize into puncta in intestinal epithelial cells and activate the p38 PMK-1 immune pathway through its intrinsic NADase activity.
evidence: Stated as main conclusion in discussion summarizing the cholesterol deprivation findings.

claim: Priming of innate immune defenses during conditions of low cholesterol availability augments immune effector induction and leads to decreased accumulation of pathogen in the intestine during a subsequent bacterial infection.
source: We found that priming of innate immune defenses during conditions of low cholesterol availability augments immune effector induction and leads to decreased accumulation of pathogen in the intestine during a subsequent bacterial infection.
evidence: Stated as conclusion in discussion summarizing the priming effect of cholesterol deprivation.

claim: Immune activation during cholesterol deprivation represents a new adaptive response that allows a metazoan host to anticipate environmental threats during cholesterol deprivation, a time of relative susceptibility to infection.
source: We therefore propose that immune activation in this manner represents a new adaptive response that allows a metazoan host to anticipate environmental threats during cholesterol deprivation, a time of relative susceptibility to infection.
evidence: Stated as proposal/hypothesis in discussion based on the priming data.

claim: Human SARM1 aggregates and undergoes a phase transition to potentiate its intrinsic NAD+ glycohydrolase activity.
source: Loring et al. demonstrated that human SARM1 aggregates and undergoes a phase transition to potentiate its intrinsic NAD+ glycohydrolase activity (Loring et al., 2021).
evidence: Directly stated in discussion with citation to Loring et al., 2021.

claim: Loss of mammalian SARM1 protects against axonal degeneration following neuronal injury.
source: These authors studied SARM1 in the context of neuronal degeneration as it was previously demonstrated that loss of mammalian SARM1 protects against axonal degeneration following neuronal injury (Marion et al., 2019; Henninger et al., 2016; Geisler et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated in discussion with citations to Marion et al., 2019, Henninger et al., 2016, and Geisler et al., 2016.

claim: Treatment with non-physiologic concentrations of citrate led to puncta formation of C. elegans TIR-1 in neurons, which was correlated with enhanced axonal degeneration.
source: Treatment with non-physiologic concentrations of citrate, a molecule that induces protein precipitation, led to puncta formation of C. elegans TIR-1 in neurons, which was correlated with enhanced axonal degeneration (Loring et al., 2021).
evidence: Directly stated in discussion with citation to Loring et al., 2021.

claim: Human SARM1 forms oligomers.
source: Moreover, previous studies showed that human SARM1 forms oligomers (Bratkowski et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2020) and that dimerization, at least, is required for TIR domain activity (Gerdts et al., 2015; Summers et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: Directly stated in discussion with citations to Bratkowski et al., 2020 and Jiang et al., 2020.

claim: Dimerization is required for TIR domain activity.
source: Moreover, previous studies showed that human SARM1 forms oligomers (Bratkowski et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2020) and that dimerization, at least, is required for TIR domain activity (Gerdts et al., 2015; Summers et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: Directly stated in discussion with citations to Gerdts et al., 2015, Summers et al., 2016, and Zhao et al., 2019.

claim: Oligomerization favors the phase transition of TIR-1/SARM1 such that higher order structures are formed.
source: Thus, the demonstration here that C. elegans TIR-1/SARM1 aggregates in vivo in response to physiological stresses provides an important characterization of the mechanism inferred by Loring et al. and suggests that oligomerization favors the phase transition of TIR-1/SARM1 such that higher order structures are formed.
evidence: Stated as inference in discussion based on the in vivo puncta formation data.

claim: The enzyme kinetics of TIR-1 are strikingly similar to mammalian SARM1 – the activity of both proteins is exquisitely dependent on precipitation.
